Do not use parentheses.

text:
In the late summer of 1854, a terrible sickness fell upon Soho, a crowded district of London. Cholera, a disease that causes violent vomiting and diarrhea, can kill a healthy adult within a day or two by draining the body of water. Within about ten days of the first cases at the end of August, several hundred people living near Broad Street had died. Whole families were wiped out. Shops closed. Many who could afford to leave fled the neighborhood, and the streets filled with a hush broken by the rumble of the dead cart.

At that time, almost everyone in authority believed that cholera spread through bad air. This idea, called miasma theory, held that foul smells rising from rotting waste and filthy ground carried the poison. It was a reasonable guess, since the sickest districts of London did stink horribly. But it was wrong, and acting on it did nothing to stop the dying.

Dr. John Snow lived and worked only a few streets from the outbreak. He was a physician of unusual talents. He had pioneered the careful use of anesthesia, and he had even given chloroform to Queen Victoria during childbirth. He had also grown deeply suspicious of the miasma idea. During an earlier cholera epidemic in 1848 and 1849, he had noticed something that bad air could not explain. The illness began with stomach and bowel symptoms, not with trouble breathing. That suggested to him that people swallowed whatever caused it. He believed the cause traveled in contaminated water, a view he had already published, though few took it seriously.

When the Broad Street outbreak erupted, Snow saw his chance to test his idea on a small, well-defined stretch of the city. He began by doing something simple and tiring. He walked the streets and knocked on doors. He obtained the list of deaths from the local registrar, which gave the names and addresses of the victims. Then he marked each death on a map of the neighborhood, drawing a small bar at the address of every household that had lost someone.

The pattern that emerged was striking. The marks clustered thickly around a public water pump on Broad Street, where residents drew their drinking water by hand. The farther one moved from that pump, the fewer deaths appeared. Snow did not stop at the map, because a pattern alone can mislead. He wanted to understand the exceptions, and the exceptions proved the most revealing part of his work.

Consider the workhouse on nearby Poland Street, home to hundreds of poor residents. Despite sitting right in the middle of the outbreak, it suffered remarkably few deaths. Snow discovered that the workhouse had its own well and did not use the Broad Street pump. A brewery on Broad Street told a similar story. Its workers drank the beer they brewed, and many were also supplied water from a separate source, and almost none of them fell ill.

Then there was the puzzling case of a woman who lived far away in Hampstead. She died of cholera, though she had no connection to Soho apart from one detail. She had once lived in the district and loved the taste of the Broad Street water so much that she had a bottle of it carried to her each day. A niece who visited and drank from the same supply also fell sick and died. Such stories convinced Snow that the pump was the source.

On the evening of September 7, he presented his findings to the local board of guardians, the officials who governed the parish. He urged them to act on a single, bold step. They should remove the handle from the Broad Street pump so that no one could draw water from it. The officials were skeptical, but they agreed, and the handle was taken off the next day.

Here history grows a little untidy. The outbreak was already declining by then, since many residents had fled and the sickest had already died. So the removal of the handle did not dramatically end the epidemic, and Snow himself acknowledged this. Still, his investigation did not end there.

Further inquiry uncovered the likely origin. A reverend named Henry Whitehead, who knew the community well and had at first doubted Snow, joined the search. Whitehead tracked down the first known case, an infant girl who had fallen ill just before the outbreak. Her family lived at a house near the pump, and her mother had washed the baby's soiled diapers and thrown the dirty water into a cesspool close to the well. Inspectors later found that the cesspool was leaking, and that its seepage could reach the water the neighborhood drank.

Snow had solved the puzzle by counting, mapping, and asking questions, long before anyone could see the microscopic germ responsible. Officials at first dismissed his conclusions, and miasma theory lingered for years. But his method, tracing a disease through the patterns of who got sick and where, became the foundation of modern epidemiology. His map remains among the most famous in the history of public health.
